pr_title: Update the `ICommandPredictor` interface to reduce boilerplate code from predictor implementation
pr_body:
<!-- Anything that looks like this is a comment and can't be seen after the Pull Request is created. -->

# PR Summary

Fix #19391

- Update the `ICommandPredictor` interface to reduce boilerplate code from predictor implementation;
- Add the public settable property `CurrentLocation` to `PredictionClient`. Please also see the corresponding change in PSReadLine https://github.com/PowerShell/PSReadLine/pull/3639, which sets the current location when the property exists;
- Remove `UnixCommandNotFound` from engine as it's been moved to https://github.com/PowerShell/command-not-found

issue_context.title: Get the location from context shell in predictors
issue_context.body:
### Summary of the new feature / enhancement

Hello 

Having play with [predictors](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/scripting/dev-cross-plat/create-cmdline-predictor?view=powershell-7.3) I feel the need for a new feature.

It seems actually impossible to get the location of the shell calling the predictor, which is very limiting considering how useful it could be.
As an example, if I had the location, I could easily create a predictor suggesting the local git branches after ```git checkout```

### Proposed technical implementation details (optional)

IMO this value should be present in the PredictionClient, or at least I should have access to the PID of the shell. (client.Name only return PSReadLine) 

How exactly do that ? No idea ^^, But I think it would be a change somewhere in PSReadLine
comments:
> It seems actually impossible to get the location of the shell calling the predictor, which is very limiting considering how useful it could be.

It's by design that the predictors do not have access to runspace state. Runspace state is thread based, and for UX predictors must return within ~20ms or their results are not used.

> As an example, if I had the location, I could easily create a predictor suggesting the local git branches after git checkout

I believe you'll have a hard time meeting the 20ms timeout for just about any git command atm. Some stuff like this will be a little bit more possible once async rendering is implemented for predictors. That work is tracked in PowerShell/PSReadLine#3581

> IMO this value should be present in the PredictionClient, or at least I should have access to the PID of the shell. (client.Name only return PSReadLine)

It's not run out of process, so `Environment.ProcessId` will give you the process ID (as your PID will be the same as the shell's)

---

@daxian-dbw feel free to correct me if any of that is incorrect

That's correct. However, you can always get the current working directory of the PowerShell session within your predictor, by syncing with the state of the default PowerShell Runspace.

Check out the `CompletionPredictor` as an example (see the [RegisterEvents](https://github.com/PowerShell/CompletionPredictor/blob/main/src/CompletionPredictor.cs#L32) call), it syncs almost all the states from the default PowerShell session. The same pattern is also used by the `DirectoryPredictor` (see code [here](https://github.com/Ink230/DirectoryPredictor/blob/main/DirectoryPredictor/DirectoryPredictor.cs#L21) and [here](https://github.com/Ink230/DirectoryPredictor/blob/main/DirectoryPredictor/DirectoryPredictorStateSync.cs#L8)) -- it only syncs the current location, which is more aligned with what you need here. For your scenario, you don't need a local Runspace, so you just need to update a local variable to store the latest current working directory.

> I believe you'll have a hard time meeting the 20ms timeout for just about any git command atm.

Right, but for `git`, you can inspect the `.git` folder to get lots of information without needing to invoking the `git` command. For example, you can get the available branches from `.git\refs\heads`. Of course, there will be some problems to solve, such as locating the root of the local repository so as to find the `.git` folder (_which you can do as part of your state syncing_), so you need to be creative 😄. By doing this with the right amount of caching, you should be able to have the predictor work well with the 20ms timeout restriction.
This issue has been marked as answered and has not had any activity for **1 day**. It has been closed for housekeeping purposes.

I thought more about this ask, and agree it's probably the right thing to add the current path information, and `PredictionClient` sounds to be the right place for this information since the host should know what the current location is, and whether it's interacting with a local Runspace or a remote Runspace.

So, reopening this issue.

:tada:This issue was addressed in #19414, which has now been successfully released as `v7.4.0-preview.3`.:tada:

Handy links:
* [Release Notes](https://github.com/PowerShell/PowerShell/releases/tag/v7.4.0-preview.3)

review_comments: Would this make sense on `PredictionContext` instead? Setting a property on prediction client itself to set up context for the next prediction request doesn't feel like the right UX here (but I might be missing some context)

I thought about having this information in `PredictionContext`, but it's difficult to do so for 2 folds of reasons:
1. The `PredictionContext` is constructed within `CommandPrediction.PredictInputAsync`, which is a static API. So, to get the current location, you will have to use `Runspace.DefaultRunspace`, which is not guaranteed to exist on the calling thread. Also, it makes it hard to check if the host is currently in a nested prompt talking to a remote session.

2. Having the current location information in `PredictionContext` means we need to retrieve that information every time when `CommandPrediction.PredictInputAsync` is invoked, namely for every keystroke when the user is editing the current command line. That will be a lot of unnecessary work because the current location won't change after the PowerShell host calls into PSReadLine, so it's always the same while user is still editing the current line.

The information about both the current location and whether the host is talking to a remote Runspace is very easy to get in PSReadLine itself, and we only need to update the information once per every call to `PSReadLine.ReadLine` and use that for all the `PredictInputAsync` calls before returning from `PSReadLine.ReadLine`.

`PredictionClient` essentially is information about the host and the information the host can provides. Even though the current location is an engine state, the host can easily access it and has the knowledge to decide whether to provide this information (_don't set the current location when a remote Runspace is pushed, as the local location doesn't help for command lines that are going to run in the remote Runspace_). That's why I decided to have the `CurrentLocation` property in `PredictionClient`.
Ah yep that's the missing context, makes sense to me. Thanks for the explanation, I'll mark this resolved ❤️
It's really nice that you can do this and it doesn't mess with the polyfill for 5.1 at all. Makes sense as the signatures are probably unchanged but still neat!
The interface default implementation is really handy 😄
